meta_description: Hybrid & Multicloud Architecture from Dataq Software: scope, delivery pattern, platforms and committed outcomes.

blocks.x: One operating model across clouds and on-premises: workload placement by signed policy, portable patterns instead of dialects, egress budgets that hold, and identity seams that work — so the estate behaves like one system, not three vendors' territories.
Multicloud is an operating-model problem the vendors will not solve for you

Multicloud done badly is three estates, three security models and three bills. Done well, it is a placement policy — workloads run where latency, data gravity and cost say they should — on top of portable patterns: containers, IaC, and a control plane that treats the clouds as fleets, not countries.

The practice covers the architecture (placement, connectivity, identity spanning), the operating model (one policy language, one observability fabric), and the honest tradeoffs — because some workloads should never leave a specific cloud, and pretending otherwise costs more later.
Below: the failure modes that make hybrid estates tribal, the reference architecture of placement by policy, and the console that proves parity.
Four failure modes that make hybrid estates tribal
Each of these costs money or uptime in ways nobody attributes — the countermeasures make placement, parity and egress contractual rather than folklore.

widgets.title: The multicloud fabric — click nodes for the consistency contract

nodes.label: Federated identity
nodes.detail: Workload identity federation across clouds — no static keys anywhere; human access through one authentication story with per-cloud policy.

nodes.label: Mesh & gateways
nodes.detail: Cross-cloud calls observed, policy-checked and encrypted; latency budgets per route measured on production shapes.

nodes.label: Interconnect fabric
nodes.detail: Redundant private paths with measured failover; the internet is the backup, and the backup is drilled.

nodes.label: Authoritative zones
nodes.detail: Each data domain has exactly one writer region; everything else reads replicated state with declared staleness.

nodes.label: Replication plane
nodes.detail: Replication with lag tolerance per domain; reconciliation jobs prove totals daily — drift of any size is an incident.

nodes.label: Placement policy
nodes.detail: Policy-as-code at deploy time: residency, latency, maturity, exit cost — a workload without a stated class does not deploy.

nodes.label: Exit plans
nodes.detail: Per-workload exit cost documented with the design choices that keep it honest — leverage is engineered, not negotiated annually.

widgets.note: Click nodes for the contract each layer offers. The consistency plane is the architecture; the clouds are plumbing.

widgets.title: Replication what-if — lag tolerance vs workload classes
widgets.note: Stale-read risk scales with cross-cloud writes divided by lag tolerance — the design answer is usually single-writer domains, not heroic replication. The curve shows why.

Identity-seam governance overlay
